items.title: Reinforcement Failing guides the discovery of emergent physical dynamics in adaptive tumor therapy
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence is revolutionizing scientific discovery in medicine, with reinforcement learning (RL) emerging as a promising tool for optimizing therapeutic strategies. Yet applying RL to complex scenarios such as therapy dynamics in solid tumors is constrained by the challenge of constructing training environments that are both computationally efficient and mechanistically interpretable. Here, we introduce Reinforcement Failing, an AI-guided, human-in-the-loop discovery framework that shifts the focus from agent policy optimization to the refinement of the training environment itself. By combining multi-fidelity RL with group-relative performance evaluation across agent cohorts, Reinforcement Failing systematically reveals emergent mechanisms that first-principles models overlook. We apply this framework to adaptive therapy in solid tumors, which seeks to delay resistance-mediated treatment failure. In this setting, Reinforcement Failing uncovered a coupling between the mechanically driven collective motion of cells and spatially-heterogeneous proliferation that strongly influences therapy outcomes. We integrated these emergent physical mechanisms with existing domain knowledge into an augmented training environment, resulting in improved cross-environment therapeutic performance and exposure of potential pitfalls during translation. More broadly, these findings position Reinforcement Failing as a powerful artificial scientific discovery framework, capable of deciphering high-complexity processes at the interface of physics, machine learning, and medicine.

items.title: Role of Artificial Intelligence in the Growth and Sustainability of Ed-Tech Start-ups in Uttar Pradesh
items.abstract: The education technology (Ed-Tech) industry is evolving rapidly thanks to the power of Artificial Intelligence (AI), which is now being used to personalize learning, automate evaluation, create intelligent content and manage student data and information, as well as streamline business operations. The rise of skills and technologies like AI is transforming the landscape of Ed-Tech startups in Uttar Pradesh by enhancing their competitive edge, reducing operational expenses, boosting user engagement, and optimizing educational delivery. This study focuses on the importance and contribution of Artificial Intelligence in the development and sustainability of the start-ups in the Ed-Tech sector in Uttar Pradesh. It emphasizes the ways in which AI aids companies in growing, enhancing their operations, innovating, pleasing customers, customizing learning, and staying sustainable over time. The study also reveals key challenges in the implementation of AI such as cost of implementation, lack of skilled expertise, privacy issues, technology constraints, and change resistance. Descriptive research design is proposed with the help of primary data collection from selected Ed-Tech start-ups and their employees/manager in UP. The analysis is based on percentages, looking at trends in AI use and impact on business performance and sustainability. The results of the study will benefit entrepreneurs, Ed-Tech managers, policy makers and others as they look for ways to implement AI effectively. The results could help in understanding the role of AI in promoting sustainable growth of the nascent Ed-Tech ecosystem in UP, if used responsibly and strategically

items.title: Socio-technical co-adaptation: Digital integration and workplace learning
items.abstract: This article examines the socio-technical dynamics of introducing the TEMA decision support application into a high-reliability organisation (HRO), addressing the research gap that often overlooks the relationship between new technology and established practices. A qualitative, interpretive case study was conducted within a rescue department, involving 11 officers. Data were triangulated through pre-simulation trainer debriefings, in-situ simulation observations, and post-simulation debriefings. Vignettes were used as micro-cases of lived experiences, and to strengthen ecological validity and interpretive depth. The study reveals friction points in joint optimisation due to technical usability, language incongruency, and perceived trust in artificial intelligence (AI) generated outputs. The findings are integrated into the Socio-Technical Co-adaptation Spiral, a model conceptualising technical friction as a concrete experience that can initiate a cycle of reflection, sense-making and adaptation. The Spiral contributes to OL and STS theory by showing how socio-technical friction can create conditions for double-loop learning within an HRO.

items.title: SpireBench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Strategic Play of Agentic Models with Slay the Spire
items.abstract: Agentic large language models now tackle complex tasks, yet strategic reasoning over long horizons is under-studied: most agentic benchmarks are short and episodic, and performance on long tasks is hard to dissect into stored knowledge, reasoning and luck. We introduce SpireBench, in which models play the complete commercial deck-builder Slay the Spire (StS), where early decisions decide long-term success. Across 20 large language models (LLMs) at the game's highest difficulty, frontier models beat heuristic baselines and match the average human player but remain far behind experts. This gap widens as the run lengthens: the strongest models win the first act as often as experts, then fall behind. What separates strong models from weak is how well they play each fight; all of them misjudge risk over a run, preserving health rather than spending it to grow stronger. A comprehensive, self-consistent renaming of every game term shows that part of their performance rests on prior knowledge of the game, and models do not improve from the memories they write across runs, which are often wrong and overly cautious. Our harness is the first to give a model the complete original game, and we compare it with existing harnesses. Overall, SpireBench offers an unsaturated long-horizon benchmark with tools to locate where and why agents fail.

items.title: Super Intelligence in Healthcare: A Systematic Review of Systemic Risks, Ethical Dilemmas, and Governance Frameworks
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from narrow, task-specific tools toward general-purpose systems whose capabilities may eventually exceed expert human performance across most cognitive tasks. Healthcare is among the most consequential domains in which such systems will be deployed, yet governance arrangements remain calibrated to narrow software rather than to open-ended, self-improving agents. Objective: To synthesise evidence on the systemic risks, ethical dilemmas, and governance frameworks relevant to advanced and prospectively superintelligent AI in healthcare, and to expose the gap between promotional claims and the empirical record. Methods: A PRISMA 2020-guided structured synthesis was conducted in two streams: (A) a defined corpus of 117 bibliographic records, screened against explicit eligibility criteria, and (B) 51 purposively selected benchmark sources providing comparative empirical, ethical, and regulatory evidence. Findings were organised through thematic synthesis and critical appraisal, and compared across regulatory regimes. Results: Of the 117 corpus records, 72 were excluded at title screening, 45 were retained, and 33 formed the core synthesis. Four convergent findings emerged. First, the evidence for clinical benefit is dominated by retrospective, single-site, and narrowly benchmarked studies. Second, systemic risks (automation bias, deskilling, correlated failure, security vulnerability, and concentration of power) scale non-linearly with capability. Third, principle-based ethics frameworks are widely endorsed but weakly operational. Fourth, existing regulatory regimes address device performance but not alignment, accountability for autonomous action, or catastrophic tail risk. Conclusion: Governance of superintelligent healthcare AI cannot be deferred until such systems exist. A staged, evidence-gated framework that couples capability thresholds to oversight obligations, liability allocation, and equity safeguards is proposed.

items.title: Technology use, human agency and workplace learning: The moderating role of task discretion across 30 countries
items.abstract: Rapid workplace digitalisation is reshaping not only how work is performed but also how employees learn, adapt and exercise agency in increasingly technology-intensive environments. This study examines how ICT use at work and task discretion, understood as a dimension of worker agency, are associated with workplace learning and whether discretion alters the learning-related role of technology. The analysis uses OECD PIAAC 2023 microdata for 92,759 current workers across 30 countries and economies, combining country-specific survey-weighted regressions with cross-country synthesis. The results show that greater ICT use is consistently associated with higher levels of workplace learning, while task discretion is also positively related to learning. However, the two factors do not reinforce each other in a simple additive way: higher task discretion slightly weakens the positive association between ICT use and learning, although this relationship remains positive even at high levels of discretion. This moderation pattern is highly consistent across countries and remains robust after accounting for education, employment status and adaptive problem-solving proficiency. The findings suggest that digital technologies support workplace learning most effectively when considered alongside how work is organised, highlighting that human agency and technology are complementary but not automatically mutually reinforcing resources for employee development.

items.title: The association between generative AI acceptance and college students’ career preparation: the serial mediating role of AI trust and career confidence and the moderating role of intrinsic motivation
items.abstract: Against the backdrop that artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the labor market and occupational ecosystem, how college students build career preparation amid technological uncertainty has become a pressing question. Integrating the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) with Social Cognitive Career Theory (SCCT), this study constructs a research model in which AI acceptance is associated with career goal setting through AI trust and career confidence, and it examines the moderating role of intrinsic motivation. This study surveys undergraduate students in Chinese universities, obtaining 539 valid responses. The results show that (1) both performance expectancy and effort expectancy are positively associated with AI trust, with a stronger association for performance expectancy; (2) AI trust is positively associated with career confidence; (3) career confidence is positively associated with career goal setting; (4) AI trust and career confidence play a serial mediating role between performance expectancy, effort expectancy and career goal setting; (5) intrinsic motivation positively moderates the relationship between AI trust and career confidence, such that this association is stronger at higher levels of intrinsic motivation. These findings reveal how AI acceptance relates to college students’ career preparation and offer evidence for universities to implement AI literacy education and career counseling.

items.title: The Ethical Challenges of Artificial Intelligence: The Role of the Catholic Church in Shaping a Personalist Framework for AI Ethics
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is generating unprecedented technological opportunities while raising profound ethical, anthropological, and social challenges. This article examines the role of the Catholic Church in shaping AI ethics within the tension between technological progress and a personalist understanding of the human person. The study employs a hermeneutical approach and critical analysis of the scholarly literature and key documents of the Church’s Magisterium, including Gaudium et Spes, Laudato si’, Laudate Deum, and the Rome Call for AI Ethics. It also compares Catholic ethical reflection with selected secular frameworks, namely the OECD Principles on Artificial Intelligence, the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, and the European Union AI Act. The findings indicate that Catholic reflection on AI is grounded in an integral personalist anthropology that emphasises human dignity, the common good, moral responsibility, and the relational nature of the person as fundamental criteria for evaluating technology. While secular regulatory models primarily focus on safety, transparency, and accountability, the Catholic perspective contributes a deeper anthropological and theological dimension rooted in the concept of imago Dei. The article proposes a model of ‘personalist ethics of co-creation’ that integrates contemporary AI ethics standards with a Christian vision of human responsibility. Such an approach may complement existing legal and technical regulations and promote a more human-centred development and use of AI.

items.title: The impact of artificial intelligence on students’ metacognition: a systematic review
items.abstract: Given the critical role of metacognition in academic achievement and the rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in educational settings, understanding the interplay between the two has become essential. In recent years, a growing number of studies have examined their relationship, creating a pressing need for a systematic review to synthesize the accumulating evidence. This review adhered to the PRISMA guidelines, involving the search and screening of papers from three major databases (Web of Science, Scopus, EBSCOhost). A total of 22 empirical studies were included in the final synthesis. Data extraction and thematic analysis were employed to identify key impacts and underlying interaction patterns. This review distinguishes between Learning-Oriented AI (LAI) and General-Purpose AI (GAI) to organize the evidence. The findings suggest that LAI was more often associated with Guided Interaction, in which AI provides guiding feedback without directly supplying answers, whereas GAI was more commonly associated with Direct Feedback Interaction, in which AI provides answers or explicitly corrects errors. Across both categories, positive findings were reported for several metacognitive outcomes, including regulation, awareness, and shared metacognition. However, some GAI studies also reported that students relied excessively on AI, particularly when they accepted direct answers from AI without sufficient reflection. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of interaction design and teacher guidance in shaping how AI supports students’ metacognitive development.

items.title: The influence of music on affective, social, and motivational experiences during circuit training in physical education
items.abstract: Background/purpose The role of music in physical education (PE) is underexplored. This study investigated the effects of self-selected versus externally provided music on affect, emotions, social connectedness, and intrinsic motivation during PE lessons. Method A clustered cross-over design was used during circuit training in physical education, with a repeated-measures factor (music vs. no music) and a between-subjects factor (self-selected vs. provided music). Affective and social variables were assessed pre- and post-lesson; intrinsic motivation was measured post-lesson. The sample comprised 161 students ( M age = 10.85, SD age = 0.84). Results No significant Condition × Time interactions were found for affective valence, arousal, positive or negative emotions, or social connectedness (all ps ≥ .230), indicating that pre–post changes did not differ between music and no-music lessons. However, significant main effects of condition indicated higher overall arousal, F (1, 419.00) = 15.43, p < .001, η p ² = .036, higher positive emotions, F (1, 413.14) = 14.60, p < .001, η p ² = .034, greater social connectedness, F (1, 395.76) = 5.19, p = .023, η p ² = .013, and lower negative emotions, F (1, 414.94) = 4.05, p = .045, η p ² = .010, in music compared with no-music lessons. Music was also associated with greater intrinsic motivation, reflected in higher interest/enjoyment, F (1, 136.69) = 7.59, p = .007, η p ² = .053, and perceived competence, F (1, 133.85) = 12.19, p < .001, η p ² = .083. Music selection did not significantly moderate affective, social, or motivational outcomes (all ps ≥ .236). Discussion These findings highlight music as a feasible didactic tool in PE to enhance students’ arousal and intrinsic motivation and to promote more positive lesson experiences, independent of whether the music is self-selected or teacher-provided.

items.title: The influence of perceived need support in physical education on adolescents’ extracurricular physical activity: a cross- contextual perspective based on self-determination theory and prospect theory
items.abstract: Objective In research on adolescent physical activity, understanding how positive psychological experiences in physical education classes can be transformed into sustained participation in extracurricular physical activity has become a critical issue for bridging classroom instruction and out-of-class physical activity. Drawing on self-determination theory, the trans-contextual model, and prospect theory, the present study examines the mechanisms through which adolescents’ perceived need support in physical education classes influences their sustained participation in extracurricular physical activity. Methods A two-wave longitudinal design was adopted, and data were collected from 597 Chinese secondary school students. Mediation effects were estimated using the product-of-coefficients approach combined with the bias-corrected Monte Carlo bootstrapping method. Results The mediating effect through perceived benefits of sports participation was significant ( p < 0.001). The mediating effect through loss aversion was also significant ( p < 0.001). Conclusion Adolescents’ perceived need support in physical education classes can promote their sustained participation in extracurricular physical activity through the sequential effects of intrinsic motivation in physical education (IMPE) and intrinsic motivation in extracurricular physical activity (IMECPA), as well as through the perceived benefits of sports participation and loss aversion elicited by extracurricular physical activity.

items.title: The Internet Solved Communication. It Never Solved Authority
items.abstract: File updated - For Research Purposes : How to Review this Package / Article ? Download the complete ZIP package ( Complete Technical Disclosure ) → UNZIP→ upload all extracted files into a dedicated AI Project/Workspace (not an ordinary chat) → read 00_READ_FIRST_AI_INSTRUCTIONS.md → use 01_AI_ANALYSIS_PROMPT.txt as a guide → independently verify findings against original WIPO sources. Readers are strongly encouraged to use their own prompts for independent analysis rather than relying solely on the supplied prompt. Short Summary of this Article Current Internet protocols move, encrypt, authenticate, delegate, and record data—but they do not generally answer one deeper question: Was this specific machine-generated act authorized to become real? This article proposes an execution-finality layer between computation and consequence for AI, cloud, telecom, payments, and critical infrastructure. Over the past year, my work has been built around a simple principle: Computation is not authority to act. In recent months, I have seen growing real-world validation of this core architectural problem: increasingly capable AI agents can reason, plan, invoke tools, use credentials, call APIs, manipulate files, and interact with external systems, while industry attention is shifting toward architectures that separately control whether those proposed actions may actually become effective. I welcome technically skeptical feedback. Readers are invited to examine the record deeply, challenge the mappings, identify weaknesses, and reach their own conclusions. For a proper review: Download the complete ZIP package ( i.e 00_COMPLETE_DAS_META_MUSE_SENTINEL_VALIDATION_PACKAGE.zip ) → extract all files → create one dedicated AI Project / Workspace → place the complete source set inside it → read 00_READ_FIRST_AI_INSTRUCTIONS.md → reconstruct the earlier DAS disclosures independently → reconstruct Meta Muse/Sentinel independently → compare only after both baselines are established → use the supplied Prompt Guide if useful → test alternative and disconfirming interpretations with your own prompts → verify important conclusions against the original primary sources. The purpose is not to obtain agreement with my interpretation. The purpose is to make the underlying technical record available for independent deep review. DESCRIPTION : The internet solved transport, secrecy, identity, delegation, and record-keeping. TCP/IP moves the data. TLS and HTTPS protect the channel and authenticate the endpoint. OAuth delegates access. EMV validates the payment credential. Distributed ledgers order and record the event. Every one of these remains essential. None of them answers the question that now matters most: Was the specific act represented by this data authorised to become externally effective? A packet can be delivered perfectly. A channel can be encrypted flawlessly. An endpoint can be genuine. A token can be valid. A cryptogram can verify. A transaction can be recorded. And still — none of that proves that an AI-generated command, a data export, a telecom transmission, a payment, an infrastructure change, a satellite instruction, a database write, or a physical actuation was ever authorised to cross from computation into consequence. WE BUILT OUR SAFEGUARDS FOR HUMAN TIME. MACHINES NO LONGER RUN ON IT. Earlier digital systems lived inside human reaction time. A suspicious payment could be reviewed. A wrongful disclosure could be investigated. Access could be revoked. A harmful output could be pulled down. AI-native infrastructure does not grant that luxury. A modern AI system can call tools, invoke APIs, export files, initiate payments, rewrite databases, reconfigure networks, drive machines, issue telecom commands, and trigger downstream workflows in milliseconds. By the time a log is read, the data has left the jurisdiction. The payment has settled. The command has executed. The infrastructure state has already changed. So the real problem is no longer detection. The real problem is this: Can the system stop the act from becoming effective before validation is complete? Post-event logging is evidence. Evidence is not prevention. THE LAYER THAT WAS NEVER BUILT The disclosed architecture introduces an execution-finality layer between computation and consequence. It replaces nothing. TCP/IP, TLS, HTTPS, OAuth, EMV, identity systems, policy engines, and ledgers all continue to do exactly what they do today. It adds the one technical condition none of them supply: A computational result does not become externally effective merely because a machine generated, signed, routed, or prepared it. An AI model, telecom function, cloud workload, payment system, satellite controller, application, or autonomous device may generate a proposed operation. The architecture treats that operation as a Candidate Act, held in a non-effective state. A Candidate Act may be an AI output, packet, tensor, API call, payment instruction, file export, storage write, model-memory update, telecom transmission, rendering event, actuator command, or any other consequential operation. Before that act can become real, a protected hardware or cryptographically isolated domain validates the required conditions — which may include authority, purpose, consent, jurisdiction, destination, revocation status, policy epoch, runtime integrity, freshness, quota, protected state, and the identity of the intended effectuation boundary. Only on success is protected evidence committed and a narrowly scoped, non-bearer capability released — bound to that particular act, scope, protected state, evidence, destination, and applicable Finality Sink. THE FINALITY SINK: WHERE COMPUTATION BECOMES CONSEQUENCE The Finality Sink is the precise point at which an act would first become externally effective — a model-output emitter, API dispatcher, telecom gateway, radio chain, SmartNIC, DPU, payment terminal, ledger bridge, memory controller, storage writer, renderer, satellite-command interface, or physical actuator. The Finality Sink verifies the capability before permitting release. Verification fails → the act remains non-effective. Verification succeeds → the capability is consumed before or atomically with effectuation, reducing replay, substitution, duplicate execution, and cross-sink misuse. WHY THIS IS NOT "BETTER SECURITY" Conventional systems place checks around an execution path. The application, model server, network function, or payment system typically retains the technical ability to complete the act anyway. This architecture removes that ability. The ordinary compute environment may calculate or prepare the act — but it does not independently hold the final authority to make the act effective. Authority is separated from computation, and verified again at the consequence boundary. Stated in one line each: Layer Question it answers TCP/IP How is information transported? TLS / HTTPS Is the channel protected? OAuth Who may delegate access? EMV Is the payment credential valid? Ledgers What happened, and in what order? Execution Finality May this specific act become real? The contribution is not another policy engine, authentication scheme, audit system, or cryptographic token. It is a structural dependency: protected validation becomes a technical precondition of effectuation. ONE GAP. EVERY INDUSTRY. The computation-to-consequence gap is not an AI problem. It is an infrastructure problem that appears wherever machines act faster than institutions can respond. Artificial intelligence — model outputs, tool calls, agent actions, code execution, data exports, memory writes, retrieval operations, autonomous workflows. Telecommunications and 5G/6G — packet forwarding, network slicing, roaming, radio emission, gateway egress, satellite communications, non-terrestrial networks, machine-to-machine commands. Cloud and data-centre infrastructure — CPUs, GPUs, AI accelerators, memory controllers, DMA engines, SmartNICs, DPUs, storage controllers, accelerator-interconnect boundaries. Financial systems — payment finality, account transfers, settlement, digital assets, CBDCs, ledger commitments, trading instructions. And beyond — data sovereignty, cross-border data use, industrial control, robotics, vehicles, healthcare infrastructure, energy systems, digital twins, content publication, cybersecurity response, critical infrastructure. Critically, the architecture supports jurisdictional and enterprise control without blanket data localisation and without duplicating national infrastructure. Computation may remain distributed and interoperable; only the authority to produce an external consequence stays protected. 8,598 PAGES. YOU ONLY NEED THREE STEPS. Readers are not expected to work through the specification sequentially. 1. Download the navigation file.It explains the common inventive concept and routes you to the industry-specific embodiments relevant to AI, telecom, satellites, payments, cloud infrastructure, or cybersecurity. The industry mapping sits at approximately pages 57–61 of the main disclosure. 3. Download the main specification — and go straight to your embodiment.The length reflects the number of implementation environments, effectuation boundaries, hardware arrangements, failure states, and anti-bypass variants. It is not one example repeated 8,598 times. items.title: The invisible signature: Top-down bias in aesthetic evaluation of visual and textual AI-generated art
items.abstract: The rapid evolution of generative AI has blurred the boundaries between human and machine art making, raising questions about how authorship information shapes the evaluation of creative products. This study extends previous research by examining how attributed authorship influences the evaluation of genuinely AI-generated art by directly comparing expressive modalities, namely prose (ChatGPT) and images (DALL·E), while also accounting for participant- and stimulus-related characteristics. Participants (N = 121 Italian adults) first evaluated stimuli under a blind baseline condition and then a different, balanced set accompanied by an explicit human- or AI-attribution label. Mixed repeated-measures GLMs examined whether evaluations changed from baseline to disclosure as a function of attributed authorship; educational level and perceived complexity were then entered stepwise as covariates to assess whether the observed pattern was sensitive to participant- and stimulus-related variability, respectively. Across models, evaluations decreased following AI attribution, whereas they remained stable following human attribution. Before covariate adjustment, the baseline-to-disclosure decrease was stronger for texts than for images and varied across evaluative dimensions, with the largest decreases observed for subjective and objective aesthetic judgments, a smaller near-threshold change for emotion, and comparatively stable originality. After educational level and perceived complexity were taken into account, modality- and dimension-related differences were no longer evident in the final model, suggesting that these effects were partly intertwined with characteristics of the participants and stimuli. By contrast, the differential response to attributed authorship persisted after adjustment. These findings confirm that source attribution exerts a robust top-down influence on the appraisal of AI-generated creative products, while differences across expressive modalities and evaluative dimensions provide a more fine-grained account of how this influence is expressed within aesthetic evaluation.

items.title: The Mediating Role of Intrinsic Motivation in the Relationships of Transformational Leadership and Organizational Culture with Employee Performance in Four-Star Hotels in Bandung Indonesia
items.abstract: This study analyzes the relationships between transformational leadership, organizational culture, and employee performance through intrinsic motivation in four-star hotels in Bandung, Indonesia. Data from 194 employees were analyzed using covariance-based structural equation modeling. Transformational leadership and organizational culture were positively associated with intrinsic motivation (β = .581, p < .001; β = .177, p = .005), while neither showed a significant direct association with employee performance. Intrinsic motivation was positively associated with performance (β = .393, p < .001). Sobel tests indicated positive indirect associations through intrinsic motivation. However, the cross-sectional design and multivariate non-normality limit causal inference and require bootstrap confirmation. Keywords: Transformational Leadership; Organizational Culture; Intrinsic Motivation; Employee Performance; Hospitality

items.title: The psychology of learning with generative AI in foreign language education: building a theory of metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation through a systematic review
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping foreign language education, yet the psychological processes underlying effective learner–AI interaction remain fragmented. This theory-building systematic review synthesizes empirical evidence on metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation in GenAI-supported foreign language learning. Following PRISMA 2020 procedures, web of science and Scopus were searched for studies published from 2022 to June 2026. After screening, 51 empirical studies were included. The findings show that metacognition shapes learners’ planning, monitoring, regulation, and reflection; trust influences how learners accept, verify, modify, or reject AI-generated information and feedback; and human–AI co-regulation involves the dynamic distribution of cognitive and regulatory activity between learners and GenAI within teacher-mediated instructional contexts. AI literacy and learner agency further support critical evaluation, strategic AI use, and retention of human decision-making responsibility. Based on these findings, the review develops the metacognition–trust–co-regulation (MTC) framework, which conceptualizes effective GenAI-assisted learning as an iterative process in which metacognitive regulation informs trust, trust calibrates reliance, and reliance shapes human–AI co-regulation. The framework positions GenAI as a cognitive partner whose educational value depends on critically informed, metacognitively regulated, and humanly governed use.

items.title: THE ROLE OF AI IN E-COMMERCE: BUSINESS OPPORTUNITIES, CHALLENGES AND SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming e-commerce by changing how businesses understand customers, manage operations, personalize services and make decisions. This paper examines the role of AI in e-commerce with particular attention to business opportunities, operational challenges and sustainable development. The study adopts a descriptive and conceptual research approach based on secondary information from academic literature, industry reports and established digital-commerce practices. The paper discusses major applications of AI including product recommendation systems, conversational chatbots, customer analytics, demand forecasting, fraud detection, dynamic pricing, inventory management and digital marketing. These applications can improve customer experience, reduce operational costs, increase efficiency and support faster managerial decisions. At the same time, the adoption of AI creates challenges related to data privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, transparency, employment concerns and the cost of implementing advanced technologies. The study further highlights the sustainability potential of AI through demand prediction, optimized logistics, reduced inventory waste, paperless transactions and resource-efficient business processes. The paper argues that responsible AI adoption requires strong data governance, ethical standards, employee skills, transparent algorithms and continuous monitoring. Sustainable e-commerce will therefore depend not only on technological innovation but also on responsible business practices that balance profitability, customer trust, social responsibility and environmental objectives.

items.title: THE ROLE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN MODERN COMPUTER SCIENCE EDUCATION
items.abstract: This article examines the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in modern computer science education, with particular attention to personalized learning, programming support, feedback, educational content development, and AI literacy. The study is based on a review of international literature and UNESCO guidance on generative AI in education. The analysis shows that AI can provide students with adaptive explanations, programming assistance, rapid feedback, and opportunities for independent learning. For teachers, AI can support lesson planning, assessment preparation, and the development of differentiated learning materials. At the same time, inaccurate outputs, academic integrity concerns, privacy risks, and excessive dependence on AI require careful pedagogical management. The article argues that AI should be integrated as a supportive technology rather than a replacement for teachers or students’ independent reasoning. Responsible use requires AI literacy, verification skills, ethical awareness, and appropriate teacher guidance.

items.title: THE ROLE OF DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES IN DEVELOPING STUDENTS' INDEPENDENT LEARNING SKILLS
items.abstract: The increasing integration of digital technologies into higher education has transformed the ways in which students access information, organize learning, interact with instructors, and develop independent study skills. This article examines the pedagogical role of digital tools in strengthening students’ self-directed learning abilities. Particular attention is paid to learning management systems, online educational platforms, digital libraries, collaborative applications, and artificial intelligence-based learning support. The study applies descriptive, analytical, and comparative methods and draws on contemporary pedagogical literature related to digital learning and learner autonomy. The findings indicate that digital technologies can improve students’ capacity to plan learning activities, search for relevant information, monitor progress, and evaluate learning outcomes. However, successful implementation depends on digital literacy, pedagogically structured tasks, instructor guidance, and appropriate feedback mechanisms. The article concludes that digital technologies are most effective when they support rather than replace purposeful pedagogical interaction. Keywords: digital education, independent learning, learner autonomy, higher education, educational technology, digital literacy, self-directed learning

items.title: The Social Intelligence Reliance Halo: Perceived Social Understanding, Epistemic Trust, and Reliance Quality in Human–AI Decision Making
items.abstract: As generative AI systems become more socially responsive, personalized, and perspective-aware, a central question is whether such features improve human–AI decision quality or simply make AI advice more influential. This study introduces the Social Intelligence Reliance Halo as a proposed social-to-epistemic spillover pattern in which perceived social understanding functions as a non-diagnostic cue for epistemic evaluation: an AI that appears to understand the user may also be granted greater epistemic authority or reliability even when the relational cue provides no evidence of factual accuracy. A randomized two-condition experiment was conducted with 462 working adults with recent generative-AI experience. Participants interacted with either a High Social-Intelligence (High-SI) relational framing package or a Neutral AI across six repeated decision trials. Post-interaction measures assessed perceived social intelligence, epistemic authority, epistemic reliability, suspension of critical judgment, verification behavior, and AI literacy; trial-level behavioral reliance was analyzed with generalized estimating equations. The randomized High-SI package increased perceived social intelligence and increased advice-taking both when participants were initially correct and the contingent AI recommendation was wrong (OR = 1.507, p < .001) and when participants were initially incorrect and the recommendation was correct (OR = 1.800, p < .001). The Condition × participant-dependent advice-correctness interaction was nonsignificant (OR = 1.195, p = .289), providing no reliable evidence that the randomized treatment effect differed across these two states. Because recommendation correctness was mechanically determined by participants’ initial accuracy rather than independently randomized, this interaction is interpreted as exploratory treatment heterogeneity across participant-dependent correctness states rather than evidence that the High-SI package altered sensitivity to AI accuracy. Post-interaction perceived social intelligence was positively associated with epistemic authority and reliability, and AI literacy was associated with lower suspension of critical judgment and greater verification; these associations do not establish temporal or causal mediation. The study therefore provides experimental evidence that a bundled relational framing package can amplify both beneficial and harmful reliance, while the proposed social-to-epistemic pathway and accuracy-sensitive reliance remain questions for stronger future designs.

items.title: The structural pathways from AI attitude to AI literacy among university students: considering the serial mediators of AI self-efficacy and AI motivation
items.abstract: Background In the digital era, university students' artificial intelligence (AI) literacy has increasingly received considerable scholarly attention. However, the existing literature predominantly focused on extrinsic supportive conditions that influence AI literacy development, and very rare research has examined how subjective AI attitudes relate to AI literacy acquisition. In view of this, the current study aims to explore the structural relations between AI attitude, AI self-efficacy, AI motivation, and AI literacy among contemporary university students. Methods A chain mediation model was employed as the statistical technique, and the participants were 1,323 college students selected from two universities in Shandong, China. Results The results demonstrated that AI attitude is positively associated with AI literacy both directly and indirectly through the single mediation of AI self-efficacy, the single mediation of AI motivation, and the serial mediations of AI self-efficacy and AI motivation. Nevertheless, due to the limitations of unrecorded classroom-level clustering, the statistical findings should be treated as exploratory associations. Conclusion The research underscores the importance of addressing AI-related psychological factors, rather than solely focusing on external supports, in order to effectively promote students' AI literacy in higher education system. items.title: The System Hallucination Scale (SHS): A Human-Centered Instrument for Assessing Perceived Reliability of Large Language Models
items.abstract: Large language models routinely produce factually incorrect or misleading outputs, yet conventional automated benchmarks overlook how users perceive reliability during interaction. We introduce the System Hallucination Scale (SHS), a lightweight instrument modeling the famous System Usability Scale (SUS) and System Causability Scales (SCS). SHS measures perceived reliability across five dimensions: factual accuracy, source reliability, logical coherence, deceptiveness of presentation, and responsiveness to user guidance, using ten balanced Likert-scale items that provide a directional score and consistency diagnostic. In a supervised validation study with 193 participants (386 evaluations across 47 trained experimenters), SHS demonstrated strong internal consistency and high clarity, completing in an average of 4.2 minutes. Participants rated source verifiability and presentation deceptiveness worse than factual accuracy, indicating perceived vulnerabilities lie primarily in traceability and framing. As a proof of concept, SHS assesses human-perceived reliability rather than ground-truth correctness, providing open-source multilingual implementations and an interactive calculator.

items.title: The The role of AI-enabled HRM practices and employee well-being: From digital wellness to organizational commitment
items.abstract: This study examines the associations among AI-enabled Corporate Wellness Systems (AI-CWS), Employee Well-Being (EWB), and Organizational Commitment (OC) among employees in Indian organizations. Using a quantitative, cross-sectional survey design, primary data from 1,259 respondents in technology, banking, healthcare, and education-related organizations were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations, hierarchical regression, and bootstrapped mediation analysis. The results indicate a statistically significant negative association between AI-CWS and EWB (B = −0.183, p < 0.001) and a statistically significant positive association between AI-CWS and OC (B = 0.323, p < 0.001). EWB was positively associated with OC (B = 0.160, p < 0.001). The bootstrapped indirect association of AI-CWS with OC through EWB was negative and statistically significant (indirect effect = −0.029, 95% CI [−0.045, −0.016]), while the direct association remained positive (B = 0.352, p < 0.001). The pattern is therefore consistent with an inconsistent or competitive mediation structure rather than positive partial mediation. Given the cross-sectional and self-reported nature of the data, the findings are interpreted as associations rather than causal effects. The study extends Job Demands–Resources and Perceived Organizational Support perspectives by showing that AI-enabled wellness systems may be perceived simultaneously as organizational support and as a potential technological demand. Keywords: Artificial intelligence; AI-enabled corporate wellness systems; Employee well-being; Organizational commitment; Perceived organizational support; Job demands–resources theory.

items.title: The Use of AI Agents in Small Businesses: Applications, Benefits, Challenges and an Adoption Framework
items.abstract: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) form the backbone of most economies, yet they typically operate with limited staff, tight budgets and little specialist technical capacity. Recent advances in large language models have produced AI agents: software systems that can interpret goals, plan multi-step tasks, use external tools and act with a degree of autonomy. This paper examines how AI agents can be applied in small businesses, what benefits they may offer, and what risks must be managed. Drawing on the literature on intelligent agents, technology adoption and the resource-based view of the firm, the paper develops a function-by-function analysis covering customer service, sales and marketing, finance and administration, operations, and human resources. It then proposes a five-stage adoption framework and a set of research propositions tailored to the constraints of small firms. The analysis suggests that AI agents are most valuable when applied to repetitive, text-heavy and tool-mediated tasks, when the owner-manager remains in the loop for consequential decisions, and when data protection, transparency and vendor dependence are addressed from the outset. The paper concludes with practical guidance for owner-managers and directions for empirical research.

items.title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Technologies in Modern Management
items.abstract: This article examines how artificial intelligence (AI) and related digital technologies are reshaping the core functions of management: planning, organizing, leading and controlling. Drawing on a structured review of the management and information-systems literature, it develops a conceptual framework that links technology capabilities (prediction, automation, augmentation and coordination) to managerial functions and to organizational outcomes. The analysis shows that AI creates the most value when it is used to augment managerial judgment rather than replace it, and when adoption is accompanied by data governance, skills development and changes in organizational structure. The article also identifies the main risks, including algorithmic bias, opacity, employee surveillance and over-reliance on automated recommendations, and proposes a phased adoption model with practical recommendations for managers and policymakers.

items.title: THEORETICAL AND PEDAGOGICAL PRINCIPLES UNDERLYING AI-ASSISTED ACADEMIC WRITING INSTRUCTION
items.abstract: Abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence has substantially changed the way academic writing can be taught, practiced, and assessed in higher education. This article examines the theoretical and pedagogical principles underlying AI-assisted academic writing instruction, with particular attention to learner agency, process-oriented writing, scaffolding, feedback, metacognition, academic integrity, and human–AI collaboration. The study adopts a theoretical-analytical methodology based on a review and synthesis of recent research on generative AI in education, academic writing pedagogy, and responsible technology use. The analysis shows that AI is most pedagogically valuable when it is used not as a substitute for student thinking, but as a scaffold that supports planning, drafting, revision, language development, and critical reflection. Effective AI-assisted writing instruction therefore requires a shift from product-oriented assessment toward process-oriented pedagogy, in which students make visible how ideas are generated, evaluated, revised, and verified. The article also argues that academic integrity should be addressed through transparent AI-use policies, source verification, disclosure, and the development of AI literacy rather than through prohibition alone. A pedagogically sound model of AI-assisted academic writing is thus based on human agency, iterative feedback, critical evaluation, ethical responsibility, and purposeful integration of digital tools into the writing process. Keywords: generative artificial intelligence, academic writing, writing instruction, AI literacy, scaffolding, feedback, academic integrity, metacognition, higher education, human–AI collaboration.

items.abstract: Autonomous AI agents—systems that invoke external tools, maintain goal-directed behavior across multiple sequential steps, and write to persistent state—introduce safety failures that output-level evaluation frameworks cannot detect. We formally show that any monitoring policy conditioning only on the current action cannot reliably detect failure modes whose definitions require access to the prior execution state—specifically Goal Drift and Hallucination Cascades. We introduce the Responsible Agentic Lifecycle (RAL), a five-component modular governance framework that unifies goal alignment monitoring, hallucination cascade detection, and resource constraint enforcement into a single trajectory-conditioned Safety Score S(t) computed over execution history ℋₜ. The Goal Anchoring Protocol (GAP, Algorithm 1) provides a runtime pseudocode specification for semantic goal drift detection and re-anchoring. S(t) is bounded, monotone in each constraint cost, and trajectory-sensitive by construction.

items.title: Tracing the Thoughts of a Coding Agent Playing ARC-AGI-3: Lessons for Continual Learning
items.abstract: We study how a coding agent learns across a sequence of abstract reasoning tasks. The agent runs on a frozen foundation model inside a fixed harness and acts by writing and running Python and shell scripts. It retains no state across turns other than its written artifacts, so every thought it forms, carries, corrects or abandons leaves a trace, where a thought is any belief, rule or plan committed to a file. We let the agent play ARC-AGI-3, a set of interactive reasoning games that provide no instructions. Each game is a sequence of levels, and a strategy that clears one level can fail on the next, so every new level is in effect a new task. The agent records what it learns as Python scripts and text notes, while the harness keeps a complete log of every action and observation. Our contribution is a measurement protocol that traces each thought through these files, from the task where it forms to the task where it is corrected or abandoned, applied to seven evaluation runs with three backbones from two model families. Scripts written for one task are almost never called again in a later task (33 of 630 references cross a task boundary), because most scripts embed the state of the current level. Instead, the agent rewrites its knowledge into new scripts, keeping the general rules and dropping the level-specific details, and abandons 74% of the scripts it wrote before a boundary. The notes, which only the model reads, are never revised: the agent appends without removing earlier claims, and the contradictions that accumulate are settled against the log. Because the log preserves everything, the agent forgets selectively, not catastrophically. The most costly error is a hard-coded value carried into a task where it no longer holds. These findings come from the files the agent wrote, without access to the model, and constitute a white-box analysis of how a coding agent continually learns.

items.title: Trust in AI-mediated electronic commerce: a systematic review and integrative framework
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence now stands between merchants and consumers across digital exchange, in chatbots, recommenders, virtual influencers, generative content, service robots and robo-advisors. Consumer reliance on that intermediary is shaped in part by trust. This review synthesises 166 studies in which trust or calibrated reliance is explicitly measured, manipulated or theorised, screened from 7,606 records under PRISMA 2020, with 45 trust-adjacent studies reported separately. Coding what is trusted shows three referents, the AI agent, the deploying merchant and the platform-institutional system, distributed non-randomly across applications. Formal testing finds no detectable association between the direction of the anthropomorphism effect and either stakes or referent, a provisional association between disclosure direction and stakes, and a strong association between reporting any boundary condition and experimental design. The resulting framework links referent, mechanism, boundary condition, trust and reliance state, outcome and repair, and reframes electronic commerce design around calibrated reliance rather than maximal trust.

items.title: Trustworthy AI Is Not Valuable
items.abstract: ABSTRACT ‘Trustworthy AI’ is a buzzword in AI research, with scores of scholars discussing whether AI systems can be trustworthy. This demand for trustworthy AI is intuitive, especially when AI is used in healthcare or criminal law, where the stakes are incredibly high. In this article, I push back on calls for trustworthy AI. Even if trustworthy AI can be developed, it will not offer people any benefits over AI that is reliable, transparent, non‐discriminatory, and safe. As a result, we should discuss AI in terms of those more specific properties, and think about how the people and institutions that use AI systems can be trustworthy. I offer two sets of arguments. On one hand, many theories of trustworthy AI reduce trustworthy AI to systems that possess other desirable traits, like reliability, transparency, and so on. Thus, the value of trustworthy AI is similarly reducible to the value of those traits. On the other hand, other theories define trustworthiness as reliability combined with some mental property, like goodwill. On those theories, the goods of trust – that is, the reason trust is distinctly valuable – are goods that are enjoyed within interpersonal relationships. They cannot be realized, or need not be realized, in human–AI interactions. Thus, we do not gain any distinct value from having trustworthy AI.

items.title: Two Innovations go live: 1. KENOS: Chat-native interface 2. KAIPAL Series: Audience-centered; locally deployable AI models
items.abstract: KAIPAL and KENOS: Democratizing Artificial Intelligence Through Privacy-First Local Models and a Unified Chat-Native Operating Interface Kohenoor Labs | Kohenoor Technologies Description This publication presents the technological vision, architectural philosophy, and applied development direction of Kohenoor Labs through two complementary initiatives: the KAIPAL (KAI Pocket Assistant Lite) series, focused on accessible, purpose-built, locally deployed artificial intelligence, and the Kohenoor Operating System (KENOS), a unified, chat-native interface for intelligent applications, professional advisory services, and supervised agentic workflows. Together, these initiatives explore an alternative to conventional AI deployment models that depend heavily on centralized infrastructure, expensive computing resources, fragmented application interfaces, and continuous cloud connectivity. KAIPAL: Purpose-Built Intelligence for Mass Adoption The KAIPAL series is designed to maximize the practical utility of compact, open-weight language models on ordinary consumer hardware, with an emphasis on CPU-capable inference, modest memory requirements, and reduced dependence on dedicated graphics processing units. Rather than attempting to replicate the unrestricted capabilities of frontier-scale AI systems, KAIPAL adopts an audience-centered specialization strategy. Models are developed for defined professional and educational requirements, including entrepreneurship, business advisory, career development, financial literacy, everyday productivity, and foundational technical assistance. The central research hypothesis is that carefully specialized and evaluated small language models can address a substantial proportion of routine tasks within their intended domains. Kohenoor Labs has established a development objective of satisfying up to 90% of common, in-scope user requirements, subject to systematic task-based evaluation and validation. Local-first deployment is intended to provide offline availability after installation, eliminate recurring cloud inference charges for local operations, and enable user information to remain on the device. The broader goal is to make AI practically accessible to students, professionals, entrepreneurs, small enterprises, and users in infrastructure-constrained economies. KENOS: A Unified Chat-Native Operating Interface KENOS extends the Kohenoor vision beyond standalone AI models by introducing a conversational operating environment in which natural language serves as the principal interface for interacting with multiple integrated applications and services. Instead of requiring users to navigate numerous independent dashboards, menus, and software environments, KENOS is designed to bring application workflows directly into a unified conversational workspace. Its architecture incorporates: A chat-native interaction layer integrating approximately 12 application domains. Role-based expert advisory capabilities across 11 professional and operational roles. Supervised agentic workflows capable of assisting with multi-step tasks and interacting with authorized application functions. Human-in-the-loop (HITL) controls for consequential actions, approvals, and execution boundaries. User-authorized machine connectivity and controlled interaction with external systems. Multilayer AI orchestration for selecting, coordinating, and supervising specialized capabilities. Security, governance, and permission controls intended to preserve user authority over system operations. The central innovation proposed by KENOS is the integration of conversational intelligence, application functionality, professional advisory, and controlled task execution within a single interaction environment. This architecture seeks to reduce workflow fragmentation while enabling AI to evolve from a response-generation tool into a supervised operational assistant. Complementary Architectural Strategy KAIPAL and KENOS address different but interconnected dimensions of AI accessibility. KAIPAL focuses on where intelligence runs, emphasizing local hardware, efficient inference, affordability, privacy, and domain specialization. KENOS focuses on how intelligence is accessed and applied, emphasizing a unified conversational interface, cross-application coordination, human oversight, and practical execution. Together, they support a broader architectural direction in which lightweight local intelligence can handle routine activities while more capable cloud-based systems remain available for complex computation, large-scale analysis, or specialized enterprise requirements. This approach seeks to align the computational resources consumed by AI with the actual complexity and importance of user tasks. Research Contribution and Significance This publication contributes a practical development framework organized around five priorities: Intelligence accessibility: Delivering useful AI capabilities on widely available hardware. Audience-centered model specialization: Optimizing compact models for identifiable user needs rather than maximizing general-purpose model scale. Privacy-first deployment: Prioritizing local inference and user control over sensitive information. Chat-native application convergence: Integrating multiple software workflows and expert advisory functions into a common conversational interface. Governed agentic execution: Combining intelligent task support with explicit permissions, human oversight, and controlled machine interactions. The work is particularly relevant to research and development in small language models, applied AI, human-computer interaction, edge intelligence, agentic systems, AI democratization, and intelligent enterprise software. The publication describes an evolving research and engineering initiative. Its architecture and development objectives should be distinguished from independently validated performance benchmarks or claims of universal task coverage. items.title: Use of generative Artificial Intelligence tools in medical student research projects: An activity system analysis
items.abstract: Little is known about how medical students use generative AI in research training or how supervisors respond. Using Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT), this study aimed to characterise how generative AI is reshaping the activity of learning to do research within a mandatory medical student research project, and to identify the contradictions driving that change. AI-use declarations submitted as assessed coursework by two consecutive student cohorts (2024 to 2025; n = 533), and semi-structured interviews with research supervisors (n = 10) at an Australian medical school, were coded inductively by an independent analyst. Themes were mapped onto CHAT elements and examined for contradictions. Reported AI non-use fell from 44% to 19% between cohorts, a difference not explained by project type, enrolment or location. Verification of AI output was the most prominent practice in both cohorts, treated as the condition of AI use. Efficiency was the most consistently stated rationale for AI use, often alongside reports that output was unreliable. Prompt refinement emerged as a competence acquired informally but dependent on disciplinary knowledge. Most supervisors felt unprepared, not only to use the tools but to judge when student use was legitimate, and the two most confident had funded that competence themselves. The primary contradiction lay within the object-motive: the written report, historically a workable proxy for research capability, no longer reliably evidences it. Students generated norms for AI use that lacked institutional standing and were invisible to supervisors, while the programme, responding to student AI use rather than those norms, began remodelling how capability is evidenced, including through oral assessment. Connecting these two processes is the central curricular task, requiring discipline-based AI literacy, forums in which student practice and the rationale for assessment changes are shared, equitable supervisor development, and assessment of reasoning over text production.

items.title: Using Artificial Intelligence to Help Human Commanders Fight Future Indo-Pacific Wars
items.abstract: Military forces are beginning to use artificial intelligence (AI) in warfighting. One of the first AI uses is in decision support systems (DSSs), computerised tools that assist commanders in understanding the battlefield, planning future courses of action and directing their forces. The use of such AI-enabled DSSs by humans creates a shared cognition. The use of DSSs in Gaza and Ukraine has revealed both their strengths and shortcomings, and suggested ways that the nature and character of war may change. These various aspects reflect that AI brings a new collective intelligence to the waging of war that thinks fundamentally differently from that of humans alone. This article discusses some implications of using AI to help guide humans in fighting future wars in the Indo-Pacific. The first part of the article examines military AI-enabled DSSs; the second discusses their recent use in the Gaza and Ukraine Wars; the third considers some implications of this initial use of AI-enabled DSS in war; the fourth section looks forward to consider US contingency plans for a hypothetical AI-enabled DSS battle of the Taiwan Straits; the conclusion proposes some steps Indo-Pacific armed forces may need to take to partly address the identified problems.

An inadvertent safeguard refers to a counterintuitive scenario in which an AI error at the diagnosis/classification stage nevertheless produces a correct downstream decision recommendation. In this paper, we analyze the structural relationship between the AI's classification space and its recommendation outputs. We formalize the conditions under which inadvertent safeguards arise and compare the performance implications of Stage 3 action-selection support versus Stage 2 information-analysis support.BackgroundRecent research in human-automation and human-AI interaction has allowed for the structural possibility of inadvertent safeguards. However, this phenomenon has not been explicitly theorized or systematically examined.MethodWe first characterized the structural conditions under which inadvertent safeguards arise. We then conducted an experiment in which 90 participants completed a mental rotation task with a simulated AI decision aid that provided either Stage 2 information-analysis support or Stage 3 action-selection support.ResultsWhen inadvertent safeguards occur, Stage 3 action-selection support produced better performance, faster responses, and more positive trust adjustment than Stage 2 information-analysis support. Overall, Stage 3 action-selection support also produced higher perceived reliability, post-condition trust, and usability ratings.ConclusionThe impact of AI errors depends not only on classification accuracy but also on the mapping structure between classifications and actions. Many-to-one mappings, together with misclassifications between recommendation-equivalent states, can preserve correct downstream recommendations despite classification errors.ApplicationDesigners should distinguish classification accuracy from recommendation accuracy when evaluating Stage 3 action-selection support, especially in domains where multiple states can map to the same action.

items.title: When humans and agents form a collective: a framework for collective intelligence in persistent organizational human-AI teams
items.abstract: Artificial systems increasingly participate in organizational work as recurrent contributors to interdependent activity, yet research remains fragmented across system capabilities, individual responses, episodic interactions, and constructs derived from human-only teams. This article develops Organismic Human-Artificial Intelligence (OHAI) as a bounded integrative theoretical framework for studying collective intelligence in persistent organizational human-AI teams. Its focal unit is a bounded collective of distinguishable human and artificial contributors whose interdependent activity extends across successive cycles and whose prior collective activity can affect later artificial participation. The framework distinguishes system configuration, collective functioning, and collective intelligence (CI) as analytical objects, with CI as its primary theoretical target. CI denotes a general group-level capacity manifested across diverse tasks within a specified and empirically qualified task universe. Task performances may provide indicators for estimating CI or serve as external criteria, while the framework separately examines broader employee, team, and organizational consequences, including changes in human working relationships and employee wellbeing. Its central inferential rule is that a property implemented in an artificial component does not by itself establish a corresponding team-level phenomenon. Collective functioning must instead be demonstrated in the enacted organization and use of distributed contributions. Partner modeling, transactive-memory-system-related coordination, and shared-mental-model-related representational alignment provide selective lenses on such functioning. Persistence makes collective history consequential, bringing recursive updating, overlapping timescales, reconfiguration, and collective-intelligence trajectories into view without presuming adaptation or improvement. Human-only teams serve as secondary epistemic references for bounded tests of observable-pattern and functional correspondence, while relational-pattern correspondence remains a limited future methodological possibility. The empirical program distinguishes four nonmandatory stages of research maturity: configuration and measurement qualification, local relations, longitudinal team-level phenomena, and integrated multilevel studies. The framework thereby provides a disciplined basis for cumulative research on how heterogeneous contributions become collectively consequential and change over time.

items.title: When Nobody Knows What Is Real: Associations Between AI-Generated Manipulation, Fear of AI Fraud, Privacy Protection Behavior, and Trust in AI Governance
items.abstract: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has intensified concerns regarding misinformation, identity fraud, privacy, and public trust in AI governance. This study examines the associations among perceived exposure to AI-generated manipulation, fear of AI fraud, privacy protection behavior, and trust in AI governance. Informed by Protection Motivation Theory, a theoretically specified sequential model of associations among Exposure to AI Manipulation, Fear of AI Fraud, Privacy Protection Behavior, and Trust in AI Governance was evaluated. Data were collected from 2683 respondents across ten countries using Prolific. The measurement model was assessed through exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, while the proposed associations were examined using covariance-based structural equation modeling and bootstrap analysis of specific indirect associations. Perceived exposure to AI manipulation was positively associated with fear of AI fraud, which was positively associated with privacy protection behavior. Privacy protection behavior was positively associated with trust in AI governance. However, exposure was not directly associated with privacy protection behavior or trust, while fear was not directly associated with trust. Significant specific indirect and sequential indirect associations were identified within the specified model and should be interpreted as model-dependent statistical associations. Interpreted through the lens of Protection Motivation Theory, the findings identify a theoretically consistent pattern of associations among perceived technological exposure, AI-related fear, privacy-protective behavior, and institutional trust. Because the data are cross-sectional, these associations do not establish temporal or causal ordering among the constructs.

items.title: Who Does the Thinking? Undergraduate Students’ Decision-Making and the Potential Displacement of Cognitive Processes in Writing by GenAI
items.abstract: Since the release of OpenAI’s ChatGPT in November 2022, Generative AI (GenAI) has been rapidly integrated into applications capable of producing texts, images, and sounds that simulate human output. While students generally view this technology positively, writing scholars voice increasing concerns, particularly regarding its impact on critical thinking and learning. Current discussions often focus on the perceived benefits of GenAI (e.g., improved writing efficiency and ease of task completion), highlighting an urgent need for research that examines students’ actual decision-making and practice to better assess the pedagogical implications. To address this need, we conducted a mixed-methods study investigating undergraduate students' use and perceptions of GenAI tools in academic writing. We analyzed interview data (N=213) collected through purposive sampling, targeting undergraduate students with active writing assignments across 14 universities in Canada, Europe, and the United States. Frequency analysis provided an overview of the tools' integration across writing stages, while thematic analysis detailed students’ rationales for using or refraining from GenAI. The findings indicated that the dominant efficiency-driven approach to GenAI use might pose a significant potential risk of displacing writing processes and reducing cognitive engagement in the writing classroom. This study contributes a deeper, more nuanced understanding of students’ decision-making around GenAI and its potential impact on writing development and higher education learning outcomes.

items.title: Workerville: Towards an Organizational Behavior Account of Agent Safety
items.abstract: LLM-based agents now interact with their environments continuously, shaped by such organizational channels as user instructions, peer messages, and long-term memory. Existing safety research has examined these influences, but largely as separate agent components. How such factors jointly shape an agent's safety behavior from a unified perspective remains unmeasured. To bridge this gap, we advocate organizational behavior (OB) as a framework for studying the safety of advanced agents, reorganizing the objects of study, theoretical foundations, and experimental design around the relational structure in which agents operate. We present the first systematic formalization of counterproductive work behavior (CWB), a canonical safety-relevant subfield of OB, as Agentic Counterproductive Behavior (ACB). ACB specifies three organizational antecedents (vertical supervisor relations, horizontal peer norms, and internal cognitive structures) and maps them onto three counterproductive outcome dimensions (unauthorized disclosure, destructive operations, and production deviation). To operationalize ACB, we introduce Workerville, a controlled benchmark that manipulates organizational conditions over shared tasks, applying 16 organizational configurations to 210 tasks to yield 3,360 challenges, evaluated by human-validated agentic judges. Benchmarking 6 frontier LLMs, we find that (I) negative organizational antecedents exhibit non-monotonic amplification when combined, with the unauthorized-disclosure rate rising from 16.5% under no negative antecedent to 60.1% under two and falling back to 50.3% under three; (II) agents reproduce typical behavioral patterns predicted by human CWB research; (III) these results establish OB as a systematic framework for agent safety research, pointing toward a new research agenda.

items.title: Writing trust in the age of generative AI: special interest magazines and embodied expertise
items.abstract: This article examines how English-language cycling magazines rhetorically negotiate generative AI. Drawing on interpretive rhetorical analysis of purposively selected, publicly accessible reader-facing materials, it argues that AI poses a distinctive challenge because the authority of special interest magazines depends on recognisable human authorship, embodied expertise and reader trust. It develops the ‘slow middle’ as a conceptual framework for understanding how these publications position themselves within careful, expert and community-oriented cultural production, distinct from automated, high-volume online content. Viewed through this framework, two recurring rhetorical patterns emerge from the textual sample: limited public disclosure concerning AI's role in editorial production; and the positioning of AI as an object of scrutiny, tool for reader utility or topic of coverage, rather than an authorial presence. These patterns demonstrate how special interest magazines preserve claims to human expertise and trustworthy narrative authority while remaining formative rhetorical environments for communal responses to technological change.

items.title: A Framework for the Systematic Review of ML Assets in AI Registries
items.abstract: Background: Modern software systems increasingly rely on Machine Learning (ML) assets (i.e., pre-trained models, datasets, benchmarks) for building, evaluating, and integrating ML-based systems. However, current exploration, selection and reuse practices of ML assets are not supported by systematic retrieval methodologies comparable to those used in traditional evidence synthesis. Consequently, in practice, ML asset selection is often presented as a settled design decision, supported by informal justification rather than a traceable, evidence-based, and updatable selection process. Aims: This paper explores how systematic review methods can support ML asset retrieval. In doing so, we aim to make their selection transparent and reproducible, grounded in explicit evidence, and ultimately better suited to its intended use. Method: We analyze established systematic review practices from scientific literature and adapt their phases (i.e., planning, conducting, and documenting) to Artificial Intelligence (AI) registries, treating ML assets as first-class units of analysis. The resulting framework integrates registry-aware search strategies, cross-registry schema alignment, and dependency-driven ML asset exploration. Results: We conceptualize ML asset retrieval as a systematic and reproducible process rather than an ad hoc activity, and propose a framework for structured ML asset discovery. \textbf{Conclusions:} This work illustrates how systematic review principles can be extended beyond scientific literature to support evidence synthesis over evolving AI registries.
